en: When a spear was thrust, it cracked,
The spear point shattered.
'Alas, that bitch of a woman Kanykei,
The coat she made her khan!' he said.
Once he saw its worth,
Khan Konurbai wept.
Your brother-in-law Manas the Leopard
And Shypshaidar of the red whip
Jousted for twelve days.
The red spear Zulpukor,
The fitted fine-cloth cloak—
It did not pass through in the slightest.
Making a marvel for the Chinese,
The fine-cloth cloak endured.
Your brother-in-law Manas was a warrior,
A lion who shattered the world.
Another like your brother-in-law, the one God
Will never create among mortal souls
Or bring forth into the world.
When Shypshaidar of the red whip
Shouted and thrust his spear,
Your brother-in-law blessed by Kyzyr
Stood watching without a flinch.
Whipping his mule,
When that great accursed one arrived,
Sparing his life not a hair,
Upon reaching your brother-in-law,
When he struck seven blows and passed,
Your fierce brother-in-law Manas
God supported to the full.
Your brother-in-law, from head to foot,
The Manchu champions surrounded.
Your brother-in-law blessed by Kyzyr
Did not start even the slightest.
The poor soul was put to trouble.
When the Chinese came in that way,
Once he knew his strength,
Gripping his spear, pressing forward,
Facing the giant, preparing,
The one Creator God,
Him alone he implored.
The mount beneath him,
The foal of a young mare,
The Duldul among the horse herds,
The peerless one among wondrous steeds,
Was a horse to ride on holy campaign.
The most capable of the horse herds,
Akkula he struck with his whip.
When he roared and thrust his spear,
The Chinese dressed in a jacket,
He paid no heed to his strength.
The Chinese officials with hat buttons,
He paid no heed to the best of them.
Coral plumes and precious beads,
The lungtung khan among them—
Shypshaidar of the red whip
Turned his mule's head.
'Come, Manas, strike!' he said,
And your brother-in-law Manas the Leopard
He faced and stood watching.
'O my one Creator!' he said.
Your leopard brother-in-law, Manas Khan,
Thrust his spear with force.
Your peerless brother-in-law, Manas Khan,
Reached him before an arrow could.
Upon reaching him, your brother-in-law
Said, 'The Kalmak saddle's pommel,'
Said, 'Right at the very heart,'
And your brother-in-law struck as he passed.
Who had never sat to urinate,
Whose sleeve had never touched the ground,
Who did not know God exists and is one,
Shypshaidar of the red whip,
When your brother-in-law rushed upon him,
Flew off his mule.
With golden forelock and tasseled belt,
The only son of Khan Azyz
Caught him and cut off his head.
With that, the Chinese
Had their backbone broken.
'This is the leopard Manas,' they said,
And saw the full measure of his strength.
In that great campaign where blood flowed,
How many Chinese giants died!
That Khan Manas was a hero—
Even Karykan, khan of Kakan,
Had seen it in a dream.
'He will bring suffering upon the people,' he said,
'He will destroy the lands he conquers,' he said.
Esenkan's Burulcha
And Ay Zhang-Zhung's daughter Byrmyskal
Were given to him as tribute.
Word was sent among the people;
In the city of Orto-Beijing,
In Esenkan's place,
They raised Manas to be their khan.
The Chinese khan was left wandering;
The surpassingly formidable Konurbai
At this gray cloak before you—
At the gray cloak he marveled:
'The concentrated rations, the medicine he drinks—
Ah, that damned woman Kanykei
Has made them all for him, yes,
All his protection against bullets!'
Not knowing my wondrous power,
That great swine, the monks' khan,
Cursed me sixty times.
The fine-cloth cloak is a precious thing:
In a shooting fight no bullet pierces it,
In a lance fight no spear pierces it,
A great treasure that cannot be replaced.
It will be grievous if you lose it.
You will earn disgrace if you part with it;
This fine-cloth cloak left by your noble brother-in-law Manas,
Little brother, I entrust it to you!
Regard the cloak as you would him;
Do not diminish your bearing.
May I take your troubles upon myself;
Do not lose this fine-cloth cloak.
On that journey to Beijing,
Muzburchak and Khan Kokcho died;
All who met the foe there died;
The lion blessed by Kyzyr died.
The precious, valiant warrior died.
Beijing, a journey of forty months,
He called a journey of forty days.
He exposed them in perilous places;
All the mighty warriors
Your brother-in-law, gone to the next world,
Let the Chinese take as offerings.
He lost Akkula to a bullet,
Let my dear Almambet fall a martyr,
Entered Kakan and turned back,
And lost the closest friend he relied upon,
Khan Chubak.
At Beijing, where the Four Companions would not tread,
When he had sacrificed them and turned homeward,
He reached Talas stricken with illness.
The youngest of the six lions,
Your generous brother-in-law Manas,
When he departed for the other world,
I was left alone with my dark head bowed;
Your brother-in-law left me a widow
At the age of thirty-two.
Since your brother-in-law had died,
Forty full days had not yet passed;
He had not been gone forty days
When they plundered my possessions,
When together they wrought their mischief—
May widowhood perish!—
When they found their chance against me,
When they slashed my breast open,
Unable to open my treasury,
Left behind because I had not died,
Living on in mourning,
Turning back, wailing and weeping,
Of my true worldly treasures
Unable to save even a pinch,
Thus bereft of everything—
That the slaves would act this way,
I had known six days beforehand.
I, your fierce and suffering sister,
Thinking to keep it and breathe its scent as a memento,
Had worn the fine-cloth cloak underneath.
His possessions remain; he is gone.
I have witnessed God's decree;
Your brother-in-law the khan is no more.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Driving us to distraction thus,
This filthy world deceives us!
What the Almighty lays upon our heads,
Little brother, we have no choice but to bear.
To look to as my support,
I have no son from that warrior.'
Calling her only son 'my brother,'
Saying, 'Whom have I besides you?'
She made herself known as his sister
And dressed the boy in the fine-cloth cloak.
Seeing him, her poor heart was torn:
When he wore the fine-cloth cloak,
An ancestral spirit settled on him; he loomed tall,
His figure and his bearing
Towering like Khan Manas.
His majesty stood unshaken by any wind;
To the orphan left by the generous hero,
To tell him openly,
Kanykei had no way.
Again his sister poured out her grief,
Again to the boy standing there
She pleaded, calling him 'little brother':
'Again, little brother, hear my words!
There is Andijan, there is Alai;
Many have set their hatred upon you.
To your right are the Russians;
On the uplands are the Chinese;
Many are the foes who will grapple with you.
So that no bullet may strike you,
So that death may not overtake you with it,
That your sister was a fierce woman,
Know from this day forward.
I shall give you another thing;
Wear this gift from your sister as you go.'
His sister spoke these words in sorrow.
Kept in a white saddlebag,
Cherished and carefully preserved,
With many ingenious features,
The leather trousers left by Lord Manas
Were bound all around;
From the thick of the thigh downward
They were embroidered all over with steel.
Six wild-goat hides
She had cleaned and stripped of hair,
Had softened into suede for the champion,
Had thoroughly dressed and prepared,
Had lined within with silk;
Of the Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
Sixty maidens had softened them with their teeth.
When one pulled the leather trousers,
They stretched like sinew;
When one let the leather trousers go,
They contracted like glue.
At a touch they stretched softly;
When someone gripped them hard,
The hand that gripped them was severed.
The leather trousers left by Khan Manas—
(Sparing herself no hardship,
The surpassingly fierce Kanykei
Had brought them with her,
Thinking to keep looking on them as a memento,
The leather trousers of her precious one
She had brought with her.)
Pleading, calling him 'little brother,'
Making herself known as his sister,
She brought them over and on his legs
She put the leather trousers.
Beside those lay
Leather made of elephant hide.
Beyond what a king could do
Was what this hapless woman had done:
All her many fine possessions
She was giving to the boy.
Beautiful enough to satisfy the heart,
Red gold and rubies
She had set into the heels.
Employing every art,
She had had paired patterns carved,
Had had them made in Kyrgyz fashion:
'When Semetey comes, he will wear them;
If my foal has any understanding,
He will understand widowhood,' she had said.
The rump-leather boots she had made,
Your dear mother Kanykei
Now had the chance to put on him.
The wide boots he was wearing
On Semetey's feet,
Their toes curling upward,
